stories.title: The Schedule C Trap: Why Your Biggest Deal This Year Might Be With the IRS
stories.excerpt: In real estate, we’re obsessed with the big numbers, what we “gross.” We talk about ‘GCI’ like it’s the only number that matters. We celebrate the $50 million year, the record-breaking penthouse sale, and the expansion into new markets (hello, California for SERHANT.!). But, after the 1099s are issued and the dust settles, a lot of agents realize that while they were busy selling the dream, they were living a tax reality that is — to put it bluntly — inefficient. The problem with ‘playing small’ Most agents start as “solopreneurs.” It’s you, your phone and a dream. You file as a sole proprietor because it’s easy. You run everything through a Schedule C because that’s what your first mentor told you to do. But here’s the truth: What worked for you when you were doing three deals a year is a financial impediment once you hit the big leagues. I call it the “Schedule C Trap.” When you’re a high-earner filing as a sole proprietor, you aren’t just paying income tax — you’re getting hammered by self-employment taxes on every single dollar you earn. We’re talking about a potential $10,000 to $30,000 “convenience fee” that you’re effectively handing to the government every year simply because you haven’t structured your business like a business. In 2026, the complexity has only ramped up. Between the shifting SALT cap limits and the new surcharges on high-income filers in hubs like New York, the “wait and see” approach to accounting is no longer a viable strategy — it’s a massive liability. Beyond the shoe box We’ve all been there: the April 14th panic. You’re digging through glove boxes for gas receipts, charity donation receipts, scrolling through Venmo history to remember if that “lunch meeting” was for a client or a cousin, and praying your accountant doesn’t fire you. stories.title: Luxury Condo Sales in Manhattan Rise Post-Pied-à-Terre Rollout
stories.excerpt: The luxury pied-à-terre is alive and well, despite any efforts to stifle — or excessively tax — it. While the second week of August saw a Staten Island Supreme Court judge block the rollout of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax — a controversial surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million — the first week of the month saw a year-over-year rise in such sales. From Aug. 1 to Aug. 7, there were 16 contracts signed above $5 million, a 7 percent year-over-year increase when compared to the same week in 2025, according to data from Corcoran Sunshine shared exclusively with Commercial Observer. In addition, since the passage of the tax some 16 weeks ago, sales of condos, co-ops and townhomes worth more than $5 million are up 1 percent from those 16 weeks last year, and up 3 percent versus the five-year average, the data shows. Overall, Manhattan saw 302 sales over $5 million from April 18 to Aug. 7, versus 268 sales tracked from Jan. 31 to April 17. For that same time period of April to August, sales of homes worth between $5 million and $15 million are up 2 percent year-over-year, while sales of homes worth between $15 million and $25 million are up 8 percent. However, homes valued at higher prices, like $25 million and more, are down 20 percent year-over-year — but that doesn’t mean they aren’t selling. The largest contract signed during the week of Aug. 1 to Aug. 7 was a full-floor residence at 1122 Madison Avenue worth $40.5 million. Sentiment around Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax has certainly been mixed since the legislature was passed at the end of May, especially after the mayor posted a controversial video that called out Citadel CEO Ken Griffin by name over his $238 million Manhattan penthouse and caused some to speculate that Griffin might abandon the planned tower Citadel was building in Midtown and focus instead on Florida. bullets: NYC pied-à-terre tax blocked by court; luxury sales momentum persists despite April passage.
Aug. 1–7: 16 contracts signed >$5M, +7% YoY; April–Aug: 302 sales >$5M vs. 268 prior year.

stories.summary: A Staten Island court blocked NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's pied-à-terre tax (surcharge on second homes >$5M) in early August 2026. Despite the tax's April passage, luxury sales accelerated: week of Aug. 1–7 saw 16 contracts >$5M (+7% YoY), and April–Aug period logged 302 total sales >$5M vs. 268 same period prior year. Sales in the $5M–$15M band up 2% YoY.
stories.impact: For Manhattan multifamily: regulatory uncertainty on high-net-worth buyer taxation is clearing, likely to stabilize foreign/wealthy investor confidence. However, pied-à-terre demand drives condo/coop markets, not rental multifamily; limited direct impact on apartment supply or renter demand in core Manhattan or outer boroughs.

stories.title: AV Management Nabs SoHo Mixed-Use for $43M
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the sale of 73-75 Sullivan St., a newly constructed mixed-use property totaling 32,957 square feet and comprising 11 residential units and a ground-floor commercial space anchored by The Montessori School. The final sale price was $43,333,000. A Cushman & Wakefield team of Dylan Walsh, Niko Nicolaou, Ryan Dowd and Andrew Berry represented the seller, 73-75 Sullivan Partners-1, LLC, and procured the buyer, AV Management. “This sale underscores the continued demand for high-quality multifamily assets in core Manhattan neighborhoods,” said Walsh. “The property’s fully free-market status and prime SoHo location generated strong investor interest, reflecting the enduring strength of New York’s multifamily investment market.” The property benefits from immediate access to multiple subway lines, including the C, E, 1 and 6 trains. Residents and commercial tenants enjoy proximity to world-class retail, dining and cultural destinations, as well as convenient access to parks, fitness centers and grocery stores, Cushman & Wakefield said. stories.title: U.S. Multifamily Gains Momentum in Q2 2026 as Absorption Surges
stories.excerpt: The U.S. multifamily market gained momentum in the second quarter of 2026 as apartment demand accelerated and new construction continued to moderate, CBRE said Wednesday. Net absorption of 167,500 units nearly doubled the Q1 tally, while the national multifamily vacancy rate declined by 50 basis points quarter-over quarter to 4.3%, below its long-term average of approximately 5.0%. New supply growth continued to ease, with 77,700 units delivered in Q2 2026, a 14% decrease from a year earlier. Average monthly rent rose 0.5% year-over-year and 1.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,257 in Q2 2026. Multifamily investment volume totaled $34.9 billion in Q2 2026, down 2.7% from a year earlier. Even so, the multifamily sector remained the largest property sector for commercial real estate investment during the quarter, accounting for 27% of total volume. “The supply wave in the U.S. multifamily sector is cresting, with deliveries down 14% year-over-year and absorption nearly doubling quarter-over-quarter,” said Kelli Carhart, head of multifamily capital markets for CBRE. “Multifamily is positioned for its strongest rent recovery since 2022.” Where the apartment industry connects. stories.summary: CBRE reports U.S. multifamily market strengthening in Q2 2026. Net absorption surged to 167,500 units—nearly double Q1—while new supply slowed 14% year-over-year to 77,700 units. National vacancy rate fell 50 bps quarter-over-quarter to 4.3%, below 5% long-term average. Average rent rose 1.5% QoQ to $2,257. Multifamily remained largest CRE investment sector at $34.9B (27% of volume), though down 2.7% YoY.
stories.impact: CRITICAL INFLECTION POINT FOR DEVELOPMENT: Supply wave is cresting nationally. With absorption nearly doubling and deliveries decelerating, rent growth is accelerating toward 'strongest recovery since 2022' per CBRE. Developers should aggressively underwrite pipeline assets and land in supply-constrained/high-absorption metros (e.g., Sunbelt secondary markets) before institutional cap-rate compression eliminates underwriting arbitrage. Financing windows may narrow if rates tick up; move forward on capital raises and pre-leasing near-term.

stories.title: Institutional Investor Snares San Dimas Light Industrial Park
stories.excerpt: SRS Real Estate Partners arranged the $41-million sale of San Dimas Commerce Center, a 19-building light industrial park located at 410-490 W. Arrow Hwy. in San Dimas. VP Dave Faris and EVP and senior managing principal Richard Schwartz represented the seller, San Dimas BP LLC. The buyer is an institutional investor with a national presence. Situated on 10.54 acres, San Dimas Commerce Center totals approximately 179,345 square feet and was 90% occupied at the time of sale. It is leased to more than 70 local and regional businesses, including several long-term occupants. “San Dimas Commerce Center offers the type of infill small-bay industrial product institutional investors seek but seldom have the opportunity to acquire,” said Faris. “The property combines diversified income from a broad tenant base with the long-term flexibility to sell individual buildings to owner-users. stories.title: Morris Heights Seniors Housing Project Secures Permits
stories.excerpt: Permits have been approved for a new 10-story affordable senior housing development at 105 W. Tremont Ave. in the Morris Heights neighborhood of the Bronx. Developed by Crown Holdings in partnership with The Community Builders, one of the nation’s largest affordable housing organizations, the project will provide 95 Affordable Independent Residences forSeniors (AIRS) and form part of a broader neighborhood regeneration initiative in Morris Heights. Designed by Crown Architecture, the approximately 55,000-square-foot, 100-foot-tall building will bring housing and support services to a borough where demand for affordable homes outpaces supply. In addition to housing, residents will have access to onsite amenities and services that include community and recreational spaces, an outdoor patio and garden, consultation rooms, laundry facilities, bicycle storage and a 24-hour attended receptionThe project incorporates a strong sustainability agenda through its Passive House design standards. The all-electric building will also feature an approximately 1,800-square-foot rooftop solar array. Rendering courtesy of Crown Architecture. Where the apartment industry connects. For-profit developers should monitor Bronx entitlement and financing trends—affordable + mixed-income projects may unlock faster approvals and tax credits, accelerating land-to-revenue conversion.

stories.title: Fully Leased Chula Vista Retail Fetches $30M
stories.excerpt: JLL Capital Markets arranged the $30.4-million sale of Terra Nova Plaza, a fully leased, 96,114-square-foot retail property positioned within a 301,000-square-foot regional shopping center in Chula Vista. Senior managing director Gleb Lvovich, managing director Daniel Tyner and senior managing director Geoff Tranchina. represented the seller, a global investment manager. Located at 390 E H St., Terra Nova Plaza sits within a high-performing grocery-anchored center. Dick’s Sporting Goods operates from a 44,477-square-foot space, while Floor & Decor occupies 51,637 square feet under long-term leases. stories.title: TikTok Tells U.S. Employees to Return to Office 5 Days a Week
stories.excerpt: TikTok’s work-from-home era is scrolling to an end. The ByteDance-owned social media platform has instructed its U.S. employees to return to the office five days a week, sources told Business Insider. The change impacts the company’s hybrid employees that are currently allowed to work from home at least one day per week. TikTok alerted employees across several large divisions in December to expect a full office return in 2026, according to Insider, although certain teams, like TikTok’s e-commerce division, resumed five-day office attendance more than a year ago. TikTok employs thousands of U.S. employees across dozens of metro office locations, including its Culver City headquarters in Greater Los Angeles, and a seven-floor spread at the Durst Organization’s One Five One tower in Manhattan’s Times Square. TikTok earlier this month announced the closure of its 250-person Nashville office, however, just two years since opening. Return-to-office policies have been gaining ground across the country and across industries this year, Commercial Observer previously reported. U.S. office visits rose 6 percent year-over-year in the first half of 2026, and achieved the narrowest first-half gap from pre-pandemic levels thus far. The return-to-office wave has continued to buoy post-pandemic office leasing in cities like New York, where returning demand has driven rents to record highs this year. TikTok’s move to reign in work-from-home follows similar moves by its competitors Instagram and Amazon. Amazon’s office workers returned for five-day work weeks nearly two years ago, while other large technology companies, like YouTube and Patreon, have maintained their hybrid schedules. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: TikTok mandates 5-day office return for U.S. hybrid employees in 2026; announced December 2025.
Company operates thousands of U.S. employees across major metros: Culver City HQ (LA), 7 floors at One Five One (Manhattan Times Square).
Recent closure of 250-person Nashville office (opened ~2 years prior) complicates office consolidation narrative.
stories.summary: TikTok (ByteDance) has instructed U.S. employees to return to office five days per week in 2026, reversing hybrid policies. E-commerce division resumed full in-office work >1 year ago. Company employs thousands across dozens of metro locations including Culver City HQ (Los Angeles) and seven floors of Manhattan's One Five One (Durst Organization, Times Square). However, TikTok closed its 250-person Nashville office in January 2026 after just two years.
stories.impact: Mixed signal for office real estate but potential upside for multifamily in LA and Manhattan. TikTok's LA consolidation around Culver City HQ could drive talent in-migration and demand for rental housing in LA's tech corridor (West LA, Culver City, Santa Monica markets). Manhattan Times Square footprint stabilization supports office-adjacent multifamily. However, Nashville office closure signals caution on remote tech hubs; developers should de-weight Nashville as a growth lever and focus on coastal tech/finance metros with established employment bases.

stories.title: Blackstone Snaps Up Ken Griffin’s 125 Worth Avenue in Palm Beach for $86M
stories.excerpt: Billionaire Ken Griffin just parted ways with his last remaining retail property on Worth Avenue in Palm Beach, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Blackstone Real Estate has agreed to acquire the three-story office and retail building at 125 Worth Avenue, owned by Griffin since 2023, for $86 million in an all-cash deal, sources familiar with the trade said. Griffin previously bought the roughly 50,000-square-foot property from Dreyfuss Management and Frisbie Group for $83 million in 2023. “High-street retail continues to experience strong fundamentals, and Palm Beach represents one of the highest performing luxury retail markets in North America,” Elena Clarfield, principal at Blackstone Real Estate, told Commercial Observer. Indeed, as a retail corridor, the world famous Worth Avenue enjoys extreme scarcity when it comes to supply, coupled with soaring demand from a deluge of high-income residents into Palm Beach. Limited supply has also driven up property valuations in the prestigious area, evidenced by Acadia Realty Trust’s March 2026 acquisition of 225 Worth Avenue, leased to Gucci, for $43 million, or more than $4,329 per square foot. Blackstone declined to comment further but sources said the firm now intends to renovate the property, upgrading both the retail and office components to better align them with the continued evolution of Worth Avenue, a high-scale shopping district that’s home to several luxury tenants including Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Ferragamo and Van Cleef & Arpels. Representatives for Griffin could not immediately be reached for comment. The transaction represents Griffin’s second disposition on Worth Avenue in under a year. Last November, the billionaire sold his 48,578-square-foot property at 151 Worth Avenue to the family of GoldenTree Asset Management financier Steven Tananbaum, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Strong retail/commercial fundamentals and rising property values indicate healthy local economy—rent growth tailwinds in adjacent multifamily. Consider mixed-use development or condo-conversion plays in Palm Beach/Miami submarkets where retail anchors drive foot traffic and tenant willingness to pay.

stories.title: Fund Administrator Hanover Park Inks 19K-SF Deal at 387 Park Avenue South
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven fund administrator is moving its headquarters to TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Avenue South, Commercial Observer has learned. Hanover Park signed a 19,269-square-foot lease on the entire 10th floor of the NoMad property, marking its fifth office move in two years, according to CEO Chris Hladczuk. The firm’s most recent office address is listed on its website as 115 East 23rd Street. TF Cornerstone did not immediately provide the asking rent or the length of the lease, but the average asking rent for office space in Midtown South was $85.73 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “Existing tenants are choosing to expand here and new companies are choosing to locate here,” Joe Lanzilotta, director of commercial asset management at TF Cornerstone, said in a statement. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” It is unclear who represented the tenant in the transaction, but Cushman & Wakefield’s Ethan Silverstein handled negotiations on behalf of the landlord in the deal signed in July. It’s unclear who represented the tenant. “The combination of TF Cornerstone’s long-term investment, highly efficient 20,000-square-foot floor plates and premier NoMad location continues to resonate with tenants,” Silverstein said in a statement. “The recent leasing activity demonstrates that companies are prioritizing best-in-class buildings, and with one full floor becoming available this fall, the property remains well positioned to meet continued demand.” Other recent deals in the 230,000-square-foot building at the corner of Park Avenue South and East 27th Street include a lease for marketing firm PMG Worldwide, which expanded from the second to third floor in May and brought its total footprint there to 38,744 square feet, according to TF Cornerstone. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-driven fund administrator) leased 19.3K SF (entire 10th floor) at TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Ave South.
Firm's 5th office move in 2 years; prior HQ at 115 E. 23rd St. NoMad market asking rent $85.73/SF (Q2 2026).
TF Cornerstone reported tenant expansion/new company influx; property outperforming broader Midtown South market.
stories.summary: Hanover Park, an AI-driven fund administrator, signed a 19,269-SF lease for the entire 10th floor of TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in NoMad. This marks the company's fifth office move in two years (prior HQ: 115 E. 23rd Street). TF Cornerstone did not disclose lease rate, but Q2 2026 average asking rent in Midtown South was $85.73/SF. Landlord noted ongoing tenant expansion and new company recruitment.
stories.impact: Tenuous signal for office recovery in Manhattan's Midtown South (NoMad). Single 19K-SF lease to a growing fintech/AI firm is positive but insufficient to drive broad office market healing or justify new development starts. For multifamily: NoMad/Midtown South office stabilization supports nearby residential demand (grad students, young professionals), but weak overall office absorption argues against over-investing in office-to-residential conversion plays until vacancies normalize. Monitor NoMad submarket for landlord distress; opportunity may arise for larger conversion or adaptive-reuse multifamily development.
